card.hook: Come up the metro stairs and you're suddenly in a square where palm trees, a big cathedral and a neoclassical post office all seem to be competing for your camera roll. Pick the cathedral. It wins.
card.stand_here: Walk to the north-west corner of Plaza de Armas and stand on the front stairways of the Metropolitan Cathedral. Face out over the square so the palms and colonial buildings open up in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the cathedral and the open square in one frame, then go to 1x for a more natural look. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the monument or the post office dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the buildings straight, so the cathedral doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Sunny mornings are your best bet: the light is gentler and the square is quieter. On Sundays the artisan market can put stalls in your frame, so expect a busier picture.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on the cathedral's front steps, looking out over the plaza so the cathedral is right behind you. Try zoom 0.5x to squeeze more of it in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the paving from the equestrian statue of Pedro de Valdivia in the middle of the square, while you stand by the statue, so the cathedral rises behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep bags in front of your body and watch your phone, jewellery and watches. The cathedral is a place of worship and its opening status can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a few people to cross the plaza and catch them in your frame, so the square looks as big as it feels.
card.good_to_know: Plaza de Armas is where Santiago's city grid started. Pedro de Gamboa planned it in 1541 for the founder, Pedro de Valdivia. The present cathedral was built between 1748 and 1775, and Joaquín Toesca designed its new façade in 1780. The square and its surroundings became a national monument in 1986.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the north-west corner of Plaza de Armas and stand on the front stairways of the Metropolitan Cathedral. Face out over the square so the palms and colonial buildings open up in front of you.

card.hook: Look up from almost anywhere in northern Santiago and there's a big white Virgin waving hello from the top of a green hill. She's lit at night too, so she's easy to find in the dark.
card.stand_here: Face the statue so Santiago's sprawl and the Andes spread out behind her.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the statue and the city in one shot. Then try 0.5x from the base for a tall, dramatic look up, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Andes and get a tighter shot of the statue.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then drag the slider a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and she doesn't look washed out.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon or at golden hour before sunset, when warm light falls on the statue. After dark she's lit up, so switch on night mode.
card.selfie_here: Use the view terrace beneath the Virgin of the Immaculate Conception statue, at the foot of the statue. Face the city with the front camera and the Virgin behind you, and try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the statue and the Andes.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the esplanade in front of the Virgin's pedestal, a few steps back from the statue's base, so the whole statue fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The summit is a place of worship, so keep a respectful distance during services. Bring water, because the climb up is a bit of a trek. The funicular and cable car may have set hours, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the Virgin on one side of the frame and the Andes on the other, and see if you can make it look like she's keeping an eye on the city.
card.good_to_know: San Cristóbal Hill rises about 300 metres above northern Santiago and tops out at 880 m above sea level. It sits inside the Parque Metropolitano, the city's largest public park. The hill has been in use since 1903, when an observatory was built here, and there's a small chapel inside the pedestal where Pope John Paul II prayed in 1987.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the base of the statue at the summit, on Virgen de la Inmaculada Concepción, rather than the phone icon. Face the statue so Santiago's sprawl and the Andes spread out behind her.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: a little slice of Paris sits in the middle of a Santiago park, and the whole front fits in one shot. The trees and lawn do the rest.
card.stand_here: Head into Parque Forestal, where the museum is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. Stop on the open lawns or paths directly across from the front and face the main facade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade with trees and lawn around it. Only drop to 0.5x if you're so close the building won't fit. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) is good for the central entrance and the glass dome.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the central entrance on the middle vertical line and keep the phone level so the columns don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters the stonework, and there are usually fewer people on the lawns. Midday sun can flatten the facade.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x and back up a few steps so the whole palace sits over your shoulder. Keep the building centred behind you and tilt the phone slightly up so the columns stay straight.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand inside the park facing the facade, on the side across from the museum's front, while you stand with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is open to everyone, but the museum and its front steps may have entry rules or restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a gap in the trees where branches frame the top of the building, then get the entrance dead centre on the middle gridline. Bonus points if nobody wanders into the shot.
card.good_to_know: The museum was founded in 1880, which makes it the oldest of its kind in South America. The palace opened on 21 September 1910 for Chile's first centenary of independence. Architect Emile Jéquier modelled it on the Petit Palais in Paris, and the glass dome over the central hall was made in Belgium and shipped over in 1907.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into Parque Forestal, where the museum is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. Stop on the open lawns or paths directly across from the front and face the main facade.

card.hook: Fitting the tallest building in South America into a phone screen is a bit like fitting a giraffe into a lift. Good news: you only need to take two photos to win.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at the base of Gran Torre Santiago in the Costanera Center complex. Face the tower and look up along its tall sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x right by the base, where it's the only way to fit a good length of the tower in. Walk back a bit and switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the top against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line one edge of the tower up with a vertical line so the building doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: A clear day gives you the cleanest lines. Late afternoon or dusk, when the lights come on, can look great too. Use night mode and rest your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Head to Parque Bicentenario and stand next to the bicyclist sculpture on the park paths, so the tower rises behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the tower over your shoulder. The cable car up Cerro San Cristóbal also shows the tower in the background, but it's moving, so take a few shots.
card.ask_someone: In Parque de las Esculturas, ask a passer-by to frame you with the whole tower in view behind you (the exact spot inside the park is up to you, so try a few).
card.rules_and_safety: The complex is busy, so watch for people walking through your shot. If you plan to go up Sky Costanera, check the official site for access details first.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one tilted up the tower's tall sides, one stepping back with the whole thing and sky around it. Then pick a winner (or let a passer-by in the foreground show off the scale).
card.good_to_know: Locals often just call it "the Costanera". It rises 300 metres with more than 60 storeys. Building began in June 2006, paused in 2009 during the Great Recession, and finished in 2013. The Sky Costanera observation deck opened on the top floors in 2015.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at the base of Gran Torre Santiago in the Costanera Center complex. Face the tower and look up along its tall sides.

card.hook: You can't get close to La Moneda. It's gated and guarded, and that's fine, because the long white front looks best from across the square anyway. The statue-lined forecourt leads your eye straight to it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de la Constitución, on the north side, facing the main façade. The palace lies to the south and is about 2 minutes on foot away, and you don't need to walk any closer for the main view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if the whole front won't fit, then try 1x for a more natural look. Use zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for flags, statues and details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the palace, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white walls keep their detail instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Early morning gives soft light, and evening is lovely when the palace is lit. Late afternoon golden hour works too. It's liveliest during the changing of the guard, so check the schedule before you go, because times vary between guides.
card.selfie_here: Try Plaza de la Ciudadanía by the reflecting pools, south of the palace, with the south façade behind you. Or stand among the flags and statues on the Plaza de la Constitución side by the main entrance. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the palace over your shoulder. Check on arrival that it really fits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the open Plaza de la Ciudadanía, facing the south façade, and ask them to step back until the whole building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos from the surrounding plazas and streets are fine, but access near the palace may be restricted for security. Keep back from the barriers, and expect staff to ask you to move away from the entrances.
card.challenge: Line up the roofline with a gridline, tuck one statue into the edge of the frame, and see if you can make a palace look even calmer than it already does.
card.good_to_know: La Moneda began as the colonial mint, designed by Italian architect Joaquín Toesca. Building started in 1784 and it opened in 1805. Coins were struck here until 1929, and it became the seat of government in 1845.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de la Constitución, on the north side, facing the main façade. The palace lies to the south and is about 2 minutes on foot away, and you don't need to walk any closer for the main view.

card.hook: Right in the middle of Santiago, a small green island of stairways, terraces and fountains pops up between the city streets. Your easiest photo is waiting at the bottom, before you climb a single step.
card.stand_here: Stand on Terraza Neptuno, the lower terraces at the Fuente de Neptuno. Face the hill, which is to the north, so the fountain fills the foreground and the green, staired slopes rise behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the fountain with the slopes behind it. If the fountain and stairs won't fit, tap zoom 0.5x. Save zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for carved details and the yellow and white facades higher up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fountain on the lower third with the stairs and greenery above it, and keep your phone level so the steps don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer, according to one photo guide. If you're climbing to the summit, don't count on seeing the Andes, because smog can hide them on many days. Treat the mountains as a bonus.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Neptune Fountain, just after the first set of stairs on the Alameda side of the hill. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold your phone so the fountain and the hill sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the Alameda sidewalk across from the fountain while you stand by the fountain, so the water and the slope of the hill are both behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Guards at the entrance gates may ask you to sign a visitor log with your name and passport or ID number. The stairs are very irregular, so take care if you need firm footing, and keep your belongings secure while you pose. Part of the climb has been reported closed for maintenance and the park closes in the evening, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the fountain, the stairs and a good slice of green into one frame with no leaning steps, then try a Live Photo to catch the moving water.
card.good_to_know: The hill stands 69 metres above the streets around it. Much of its look comes from a big remodelling in 1872 led by Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, which gave it the yellow and white facades, the winding road and the summit chapel. Pedro de Valdivia took the hill in 1540, and a cannon is traditionally fired at noon.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Terraza Neptuno, the lower terraces at the Fuente de Neptuno. Face the hill, which is to the north, so the fountain fills the foreground and the green, staired slopes rise behind it.

card.hook: Walk down a quiet Bellavista backstreet and a bright blue wall with a grinning sunflower-face sign jumps out at you. That's La Chascona, and it's one of the easiest photo wins in Santiago.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, in front of the blue entrance wall of La Chascona on Fernando Márquez de la Plata. Face the wall so the sunflower sign and the front door are both in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x with the blue wall and sign filling the frame, then shuffle sideways to bring in the door. Want the whole facade? Try 0.5x and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. 2x is handy for tightening things up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the sunflower sign on one of the upper crossing points with the door lower down, and tap the blue wall; if the blue looks washed out, slide it a touch darker.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft and the pavement isn't busy, so you can shoot without strangers wandering through. A quieter moment makes that blue wall look even better.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the bright blue entrance wall where the house logo is painted, use the front camera, and let the bold blue do the work behind you. If you go into the museum, the garden is another popular selfie spot, with plants, an emerald garden orb and terrace walls behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the entrance walkway on Fernando Márquez de la Plata, facing the blue wall, while you pose in front of it, so they can fit the house front and upper levels in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos aren't allowed inside the house, but the garden and outdoor spaces are fine. Sources disagree on indoor photos, so check the museum's current rules and ask staff on arrival. The house climbs a slope with narrow staircases, low doorways and split levels, so the upper rooms aren't wheelchair accessible.
card.challenge: Can you get the sunflower, the door and your own grin in one frame without anyone else sneaking in?
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1953, when the house was meant as a home for Matilde Urrutia, Neruda's secret lover at the time. She later became his third wife. 'Chascona' is Chilean Spanish for tangled hair, a nod to her curly red hair. After Neruda died in 1973 the house was damaged during the military coup, and Urrutia restored it. It's now a museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, in front of the blue entrance wall of La Chascona on Fernando Márquez de la Plata. Face the wall so the sunflower sign and the front door are both in your frame.

card.hook: Most churches make you crane your neck from a narrow street. Here, the Plaza de Armas lets you step back until the whole cathedral fits on your screen.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Plaza de Armas, right in front of the cathedral's main facade. The cathedral lies to the south-west of the point, so face south-west and let the front fill your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the whole facade and the open plaza. Switch to 1x for a natural look at the front, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the details up high.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out and the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Morning light is said to suit the facade's details. If you're around later, dusk can add a warmer tone.
card.selfie_here: Head for the bronze equestrian statue of Pedro de Valdivia on the Plaza de Armas and stand beside it, with the cathedral rising behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit the facade in, and hold the phone a little higher than usual.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out in the square facing the cathedral's front, ideally in morning light, while you stand in front of the facade so the whole building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Non-flash photography is reported to be allowed inside, but flash may not be, so switch it off and check the rules on site. The cathedral is a working place of worship, so be respectful of worshippers.
card.challenge: Find a plaza tree to frame one side of the cathedral, then line both towers up with the gridlines. Can you get the building standing perfectly straight?

card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for most street scenes, since it looks natural with cafés and people in the shot. Go to zoom 0.5x for the church front when you can't step back, and zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for facades, signs and balconies.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and let the street run along them so it leads the eye in, with the buildings on both sides standing straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is the sweet spot, with softer light and quieter streets. The same light flatters the painted fronts at Plaza Mulato Gil de Castro.
card.selfie_here: Head to Plaza Mulato Gil de Castro, the small square off José Victorino Lastarria street. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the colourful building fronts and street art fill the space behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot you in front of Palacio Bruna at Merced 230, standing close to the building so its architecture fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Sidewalks can be narrow and crowded, and normal city precautions apply after dark. Keep a little distance from people at café tables. Museums, theatres and the church may have their own visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Collect a set of four: café tables, a colourful facade, the church front, and a leafy street leading toward Santa Lucía Hill. Bonus points if a stranger's coffee isn't in the shot.
card.good_to_know: The neighbourhood grew up around the Iglesia de la Veracruz, a neoclassical church from 1857. Plaza Mulato Gil de Castro was laid out in 1981 to protect a row of older frontages. Chile gave the whole area protected Zona Típica status in 1997, which is why so many old streets have kept their character.

card.hook: Picture a giant oval of city traffic with three big avenues pouring into it, and a bronze general in the middle keeping an eye on everyone. Santiagoans call it Plaza Italia, and it's the best place in town to see how the city fits together.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza Baquedano, close to the equestrian statue of General Baquedano. The centre is about 19 m (roughly 20-25 steps) to the west. Face the statue, with an avenue running away behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the statue and its surroundings. Switch to 0.5x for the whole square and the avenues, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details of the monument.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue so it stays sharp, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives the statue stronger relief. In the evening the lit-up streets around the square join the picture, so switch on night mode and rest your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Jardín de la Resistencia, the memorial garden space near the former Metro Baquedano entrance, on the plaza. We can't promise the monument fits behind you there, so treat it as a fallback: use the front camera at 0.5x and see what you can get over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography in the plaza is generally allowed, but respect any ongoing events or private property. Photograph people with discretion, don't block pedestrians while you compose, and keep clear of moving traffic.
card.challenge: Can you get Providencia, the Alameda and Vicuña Mackenna all in one 0.5x shot without stepping into the road?
card.good_to_know: The square was laid out in 1875 as Plaza La Serena and took its present name in 1928, when Virgínio Arias's monument to General Manuel Baquedano went up. The four-ton statue was taken away in March 2021 to be restored. Reports say it was put back on its plinth in March 2026, but check when you arrive. From 2019 to 2021 protesters called the square Plaza de la Dignidad.

card.hook: This church has come through about 15 earthquakes over magnitude 7, and from above it still looks completely calm, with its clock tower sitting among the downtown streets.
card.stand_here: Head up to the upper paths of Cerro Santa Lucía and look down. The church is about 550 m to the south-west of that point, so face south-west and you'll find the tower.
card.zoom: Start at 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the bell tower and its clock. Drop to 1x for a wider shot of the tower among the streets.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on a vertical line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when the soft light is said to suit the tower from the hill. The plaza facade may look best in even daylight.
card.selfie_here: Go down to the plaza in front of the church, turn so the western facade is behind you, and use the front camera. Hold it a bit low and a bit out from you so the columns, statues and carvings fit behind your shoulder. A guide recommends golden hour here.
card.ask_someone: If you want to be in the hill shot, ask a passer-by at the Cerro Santa Lucía lookout to take it while you stand a few steps along with the church and bell tower in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, so dress modestly and check the official site before you go for visiting times and any photo rules. Also check access to Cerro Santa Lucía before you set off.
card.challenge: Get the clock sharp and the tower dead straight on a gridline, then do the same with the facade columns from the plaza.
card.good_to_know: The church was consecrated in 1622, and it's one of the oldest colonial-era buildings in Chile. The first bell tower fell in an earthquake in 1647, and the tower you see today went up in the mid-1800s to a design by Fermín Vivaceta. Part of the old convent next door is now the Museo Colonial.

card.hook: Santiago's centre is busy, and this building has been quietly standing in the middle of it since 1807. Give it a proper photo and it'll look like the star it is.
card.stand_here: Start at the Plaza de Armas and walk one block west to the Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino. The phone icon on the map sits right at the building, so stop there and face the front entrance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural, straight-on shot of the entrance. If the street is too narrow to fit the whole front in, switch to zoom 0.5x and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. Then try zoom 2x or higher (depending on your phone) for doorway and stonework details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so everything stands nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go early in the day, when the street is quieter and there are fewer people in your frame. Soft daylight is also kinder to the stonework than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to the pedestrian walk next to the entrance portal on Calle Bandera (number 361) and turn so the facade is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more building in over your shoulder, and check the spot on the ground first.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone at the corner of Calle Bandera and Calle Compañía, where a photo can catch the museum's main and side facades together, and pose by the building.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the galleries, flash isn't allowed because it can harm the artifacts, and non-flash photos for personal use are generally fine. One older report mentions the Textile Room as off-limits, so check the signs and the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the passing crowd, then get one clean shot of the old building with the modern street around it, and see how long you can hold your nerve.
card.good_to_know: The building was put up between 1805 and 1807 as the Palacio de la Real Aduana. The museum opened in December 1981, founded by architect and collector Sergio Larraín García-Moreno to show pieces he'd gathered over nearly fifty years. Inside are more than 3,000 pieces from almost 100 different peoples, spanning roughly 10,000 years.

card.hook: Picture three rows of plane trees lined up like they're marching off toward the horizon, with a river keeping them company. That's the view you're after, and it's easier to get than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand on Puente Patronato and face along the tree-lined paths with the Mapocho running beside them. From Plaza Baquedano or Estación Mapocho, the park is about 460 m to the south-east, roughly 5-6 minutes on foot. For a second angle, walk to the corner of Merced and Coronel Santiago Bueras and look across the treetops toward the downtown skyline.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to show the paths and river as you see them. Try 0.5x to squeeze more tree rows in, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bunch the trunks into a tighter pattern.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the river or the nearest path with one of the lines, so the tree rows lead the eye into the distance.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sun isn't straight overhead, so the trees give softer light and gentler shadows on the paths. Early morning is likely to be quieter too.
card.selfie_here: Head to the German Fountain (Fuente Alemana), where the park's walking paths cross, and put it behind you. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold your phone a little low so the tiers fit over your shoulder. The Monumento a la Gloria in front of the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes is a second option: stand at its front side so the museum building fills the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your visit to daytime. A travel blogger advises against the park at night because wild dogs frequent it then. If you want to go inside the National Museum of Fine Arts, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a walker or cyclist on the path in your shot, so the tree rows look as huge as they feel.
card.good_to_know: The park was laid out on land reclaimed from the Mapocho River. The National Museum of Fine Arts sits inside it and shares a building with the Santiago Museum of Contemporary Art, and Palacio Bruna stands opposite on Merced Street. At its eastern end, the park carries on as Balmaceda Park, so the greenery runs on almost unbroken along the river.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Puente Patronato and face along the tree-lined paths with the Mapocho running beside them. card.hook: Picture a big red castle at the end of a small plaza, with the whole bohemian barrio milling around its feet. That's Bellavista, and the colour comes from the streets themselves.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza Camilo Mori, off Pío Nono in the heart of the neighbourhood, beside the Teatro Mori. Face the large red Castillo Lehuedé (the Castillo Rojo) at one end of the plaza.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the Castillo Rojo and the street life around it. Switch to 1x for a cleaner shot of the red building, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for mural details and café fronts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the red building's edges straight, then tap the red façade and slide it a touch darker so the colour stays rich.
card.best_time: Daytime is the easy choice for murals and the red building. A weekend evening is livelier thanks to the handicrafts market along Pío Nono, but let night mode do its thing and steady your phone against a wall or post.
card.selfie_here: Head to Pío Nono and stand in front of the celebrity portraits painted on the walls. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the colourful mural fills the space behind your shoulder. For a calmer backdrop, try Calle Purísima, where the murals and painted doors come with fewer crowds.
card.rules_and_safety: The neighbourhood is busy at night, so leave valuables at the hotel and head back by taxi or app. If you plan to ride the funicular up to Terraza Bellavista, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Keep the Castillo Rojo tucked to one side of the frame and let the plaza and its people fill the rest, so your photo shows the barrio and not just the building.
card.good_to_know: Bellavista is Santiago's bohemian quarter, dating from 1900 and sitting between the Mapocho River and San Cristóbal Hill. The Castillo Lehuedé is a 1923 building. card.hook: A little red car waits at a platform in front of an old stone station, with a green hillside climbing away behind it. Red, grey and green is a colour combo your photo gallery will thank you for.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the base station, Estación Pío Nono, at Pío Nono 450, and face the platform. You want the red car in front of the stone station building, with the track rising up the hill behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the car, the platform and the station building together. If the platform feels too tight, try 0.5x. Zoom 2x is handy when you want just the car and the track without the crowd.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red car, then drag the slider a little darker if the sky is bright, so the red stays rich.
card.best_time: Go when the platform is quiet so you can get the car without people in front. If it's busy, wait a moment for a gap and take a few shots in a row. Check the official site for running times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head to the square at the end of Pío Nono street, in front of the station. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and keep the castle-style station and its two towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the square facing Estación Pío Nono, while you stand in front of the station so they can fit you, the full building and both towers in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are generally fine on the funicular, but skip the flash so you don't bother other passengers. One visitor warns that pickpockets work the park at the base, so keep your phone and bag close.
card.challenge: Get the red car slightly off-centre with the track climbing through the top of the frame, and keep the station front lined up with the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The line is 485 metres long and has three stations: Pío Nono at the bottom, Zoo, and Cumbre at the top, where the Santuario a la Virgen stands. It opened on 25 April 1925, and architect Luciano Kulczewski designed the station at the foot of the hill. Pope John Paul II rode it in 1987, and it became a National Monument of Chile in 2000.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the base station, Estación Pío Nono, at Pío Nono 450, and face the platform. You want the red car in front of the stone station building, with the track rising up the hill behind it.

card.hook: From up here the GAM is a bit of a hide-and-seek player: a rusty-brown building tucked in among the rooftops of central Santiago. Spotting it is half the fun.
card.stand_here: Climb to the summit viewpoint on Cerro Santa Lucía and face east over the city centre. The GAM is about 350 m to the east, down among the buildings.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the skyline and the layout of the city. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) until the GAM stands out with some city around it, and keep 0.5x for the wide sweep of the hilltop.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper line, tap the GAM on your screen, and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the building doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is a good choice, when the light is softer. How clearly the GAM shows depends on exactly where you stand at the top, so check the framing on your screen before you shoot.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, so more of the scene fits in. Turn so the rusty, perforated facade or the city skyline sits over your shoulder, and check the screen before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Pickpocketing is mentioned for busy parts of Santiago like Plaza de Armas, the metro at rush hour and the Mercado Central, not for the GAM itself, so keep your phone close in crowds. Cerro Santa Lucía is free and open-air, and the GAM's public spaces are free to walk through, but some performances need tickets, so check the official site.
card.challenge: Play 'find the GAM': spot it from the hill, zoom in until it's clear, then walk down and shoot the facade straight on from the avenue so you've got both versions.
card.good_to_know: The GAM was built for a major international conference in 1972 and finished in just 275 days, with thousands of volunteers helping. It later served as a military headquarters, and a fire in 2006 led to its return to cultural use. It opened as the GAM in September 2010 and now hosts drama, dance, music and visual arts.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Climb to the summit viewpoint on Cerro Santa Lucía and face east over the city centre. The GAM is about 350 m to the east, down among the buildings.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific selfie position with the GAM building behind the visitor, or a specific spot for a passer-by to photograph the whole building. Sources describe the corten steel facade as photogenic and mention 'the main gap between entrances and any art installations' (airial.travel), but name no place. GAM's official guide names four open plazas (Central, Oriente, Poniente, Zócalo) and says the most visible one is Plaza Central, where a large wicker fish hangs (gam.cl). That is the only named place I found at GAM, and no page calls it a selfie or photo spot, so I left it out. The Tripadvisor and Lonely Planet pages mention plazas and facade detail but name none for photos. Rooftop terraces with Andes views (takeyourbackpack.com) are views from GAM, not the building behind the visitor, so I excluded them. No page gives selfie stick or tripod rules for GAM. Given the gaps, a visit to the plazas on site is the best way to find the angles.

card.hook: Torre Entel looks like a giant concrete torch poking up over Santiago, and in Parque Forestal the treetops make a leafy frame around it. Keep it simple: one tall tower, a bit of green, done.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parque Forestal and face south-west, then look for the tower rising above the treetops. You're a fair way from it here, so the park's greenery does the framing for you.
card.zoom: Zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone, to bring the tower closer, or stay at 1x if you want more trees around it. Turn on gridlines so the tower stays upright, and leave a little sky above it.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the sky stays blue and the tower keeps its detail.
card.best_time: We'd aim for morning or late afternoon. The tower has an LED screen at the top, so its crown can look different from one visit to the next, and it's worth a second look if you pass by again.
card.selfie_here: In Parque Forestal, use the front camera with the tower behind you and the park's greenery around you. For a bolder one, try the corner of Alameda and Amunátegui at the tower's base, where a Tripadvisor reviewer says the view is pleasant, especially at night. Try 0.5x and tilt up to fit the tower over your shoulder. These spots are our best guesses, not official selfie spots.
card.ask_someone: Plaza de la Ciudadanía gives an open view of the whole tower, so ask a passer-by to take your photo there with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The observation deck may not be open to visitors, so check the official site first if you want to go up. You don't need to go up for any of these photos.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the tower is the only tall thing in the picture, with leaves at the edges and not a crane in sight.
card.good_to_know: Torre Entel is 127.4 metres tall, and its shape is meant to recall a torch. Building began in 1970 and it opened in 1974, and for many years it was the tallest structure in Chile. A very large LED screen was added at the top in 2009.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Parque Forestal and face south-west, then look for the tower rising above the treetops. You're a fair way from it here, so the park's greenery does the framing for you.

card.hook: Palacio Cousiño is so neat and symmetrical that a wonky phone shows up straight away. Lean it even a little and the whole front looks like it's falling over.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Dieciocho, across the street from the entrance at number 438, and face the palace straight on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x, but keep the phone upright so the walls don't lean. Then zoom 2x or more (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the railings and tilework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the middle of the building up with the centre vertical line so both sides look balanced.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder than harsh midday sun. The street is also quieter then, so fewer people wander into your shot.
card.selfie_here: If the gardens are open (check first), stand in the entrance garden near the mosaic tiles on the ground, or beside the two iron lions, with the palace behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the palace over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Calle Dieciocho pavement facing the entrance gate, so the whole building fits behind you, and ask them to hold the phone upright and level.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the palace are usually not allowed, though some pages say otherwise, so ask staff on the day. Watch for posted signs about flash. The gardens have been reported closed or limited at times, so confirm they're open.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the left and right halves match so well you could fold the picture in half, then try to spot a window you missed.
card.good_to_know: Palacio Cousiño was built for Isidora Goyenechea, the widow of Luis Cousiño. Architect Paul Lathoud designed it in the Second Empire style and it was finished in 1878. It was damaged in the 2010 earthquake and reopened in 2015, and visits inside are by guided tour, so check for closures before you travel.

card.hook: From the street, the Mercado Central looks calm and very civic, with its neoclassical front, archway and pediment. Nothing warns you that the real show is waiting inside.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of San Pablo and Puente, where the market's front runs along the block. The market's main building is about 90 m to the north-east, so turn that way and get the archway and pediment in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front. If the pavement is too narrow to fit it all, drop to zoom 0.5x. Try zoom 2x or higher for the archway and pediment up close.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the archway near the centre so the pediment sits level at the top, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out the pediment.
card.best_time: Early morning is said to give the best light, and it's a good time to shoot before the entrances get busy.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement in front of the market's facade on San Pablo street. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if you can, and let the building sit behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working market, so check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements. Entrances get busy, so stand to one side and keep your phone close. Ask vendors before taking close-ups of them or their stalls.
card.challenge: Get the archway near the centre of your frame with a few passers-by walking through the bottom of it. Then go inside and shoot straight up at the lantern above the fish stalls.
card.good_to_know: The market opened in 1872, with Fermín Vivaceta in charge of construction. It replaced the Plaza del Abasto, which a fire destroyed in 1864. The cast-iron roof inside was made by the Scottish firm R Laidlaw & Sons in Glasgow.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of San Pablo and Puente, where the market's front runs along the block. The market's main building is about 90 m to the north-east, so turn that way and get the archway and pediment in one frame.

card.hook: Estación Mapocho is a railway station nearly 280 metres long, so your first problem is simple: how do you get all of it into one phone photo? The plaza in front gives you room to work it out.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de la Cultura, on the south side of the building, and face the main brick facade. For a straight-on view, walk west along the plaza towards the middle of the building.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole long front in. Once you've stepped back, switch to 1x so the edges look less stretched, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the brickwork, the arch and the copper roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof up with a horizontal line so the building doesn't tilt, and let the plaza paving fill the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: No special time is needed, but street vendors often gather in front, so wait a moment for a clear view. If the sky is bright, tap the brick facade and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the roof and sky keep their detail.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on Plaza de la Cultura, facing away from the station so the Beaux Arts facade is behind you. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold the phone a bit low so the long brick front fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the plaza and frame the facade from there, while you stand in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza and the outside of the building are open public space, but exhibitions and some areas inside may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole front in one shot with the roof sitting dead level on a gridline, and a vendor or two in the frame as local colour.
card.good_to_know: The design began in 1905 under the architect Emilio Jecquier. The station is about 280 metres long and 17 metres high, with a steel vault that was once glazed and is now covered in copper. It was inaugurated in May 1912 and opened to the public in 1913 for Chile's first hundred years of independence. It became a National Monument in 1976 and has been a cultural centre since March 1994, home to exhibitions, concerts and the yearly Santiago International Book Fair.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de la Cultura, on the south side of the building, and face the main brick facade. For a straight-on view, walk west along the plaza towards the middle of the building.
